title: Keeping the Evening Tutoring Pilot
text:
Northgate Community Center has offered free evening tutoring twice a week for one semester. The center director, Priya Raman, recommends continuing the program for another year rather than ending it when the pilot grant expires.

Attendance records show that 146 students used the tutoring service at least once. Of the 58 students who attended six or more sessions, 41 improved by at least one letter grade in the class for which they sought help. Raman notes that the records do not prove tutoring caused every improvement: students may also have studied more, received classroom help, or changed courses. Still, she argues that the pattern is strong enough to justify a longer trial.

Raman also cites access. Before the program began, the center surveyed 212 families; 37 percent said paid tutoring was too expensive and 29 percent said transportation to programs across town was a barrier. The community center is within walking distance of two apartment complexes and is served by an evening bus route. During the pilot, 63 percent of participating students came from households that had identified cost or transportation as a barrier.

The pilot had weaknesses. Attendance was uneven, and several students stopped coming after sports seasons began. Tutors also reported that one large room became noisy when more than twenty students arrived at once. Raman proposes using two smaller rooms next year and asking students to reserve a time slot when possible. She does not claim the pilot has already proven a permanent solution. Her recommendation is that the center keep the program long enough to measure attendance, course performance, and access across a full school year.
